sheet.title: Happy Thanksgiving from Brennan’s, 3 Courses $80: choice of appetizer, entrée and dessert
sheet.line: Pommes Purée, Sauce au Poivre, Roasted Brussels Sprouts
sheet.note: The sheet prints the dish name and its line and nothing else: no allergen marks, no price of its own (the $80 covers three courses), no method, no portion, no wine.

classic.auPoivre: Steak au poivre is a French bistro classic: a steak crusted in coarsely crushed peppercorns, the pan sauce of shallots, Cognac and cream; tenderloin or filet mignon is the usual cut; the origin is disputed, so none is given (Saveur, Steak au Poivre; Once Upon a Chef, Steak au Poivre; The Kitchn, Steak au Poivre).
classic.pommesPuree: Pommes purée is the French style of mashed potatoes: potatoes riced or milled, often passed through a fine sieve called a tamis, with a great deal of butter worked in, smooth and silky; the butter ratio varies widely by recipe (America’s Test Kitchen, French-Style Mashed Potatoes; Great British Chefs, How to make pomme purée). The version made famous in Paris in the 1980s is tied to a named chef; no person is named in the notes.
classic.brussels: Brussels sprouts are Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera, named for the Brussels region of Belgium, where they became a popular crop by the sixteenth century; the French brought them to Louisiana around 1800; Belgium became independent in 1830, so the story of a Belgian king naming them in 1820 is a myth (RHS, Fascinating facts about Brussels sprouts; The Brussels Times, A Belgian history of the Brussels sprout; Tasting Table).

sayIt: Au poivre: oh PWAHV, French for with pepper.
Pommes purée: pum pew-RAY, French for potato purée.
unsourced: Whether the kitchen’s au poivre carries Cognac or cream, which herbs crust the beef, and the temperatures the kitchen cooks it to: asked of the chef.
The origin of steak au poivre: disputed, left out.
